panels.title: Platform and alerts (what Telegram is told)
Platform layers (HTTP probe every 5 s)
panels.description: The blackbox exporter's HTTP check of each platform layer, every 5 seconds (monitoring/alerting/blackbox.yml). These are the probes behind the LayerDown alert: a layer DOWN here for two probes in a row (10 s) is a Telegram message. Prometheus cannot show itself down here; the control panel's Status tab still does.

panels.title: Alerts firing now
panels.description: Every alert Prometheus has firing now, counted by name and severity (Prometheus's own ALERTS series, from monitoring/alerting/alert_rules.yml). AnomalyDetected counts the machines on the Telegram list. An alert muted from the control panel (Infrastructure tab, Notifications) is still listed here: a mute stops the Telegram message, not the alert.

panels.title: Predictions/s by served model
panels.description: Requests answered per second, split by which model served them. telecom_v4_rolling = the caller supplied a 10-reading history (rolling features used); telecom_v3 = no history yet, or the caller never sends one. A demo agent always starts on v3 and switches to v4 after its 10th reading -- v3-only forever means history is never reaching the API.

panels.title: /predict requests/s per pod
panels.description: Traffic per pod. Kubernetes' Service load-balances round-robin, so with N healthy pods each should carry roughly 1/N of total traffic. One pod flat at 0 while others show traffic usually means it failed readiness and was pulled from the Service, not that it is idle.

panels.title: /predict latency p95 per pod
panels.description: 95th-percentile time to answer one /predict call, per pod (inference + best-effort DB write). Normal is well under 200ms on this hardware. A sustained rise usually traces to the Feedback DB write p95 panel below -- PostgreSQL contention, not the model itself, is the usual cause.

panels.title: Error ratio (4xx / 5xx)
panels.description: Share of requests answered with an error. 4xx = the request itself was invalid (e.g. history not exactly 10 finite values) -- a caller-side problem, not a service failure. ANY sustained 5xx is a real server-side problem and should be investigated immediately; 0% is the expected steady state.

panels.title: Serving pods scraped
panels.description: How many serving pods Prometheus is currently able to reach. Should equal your replica count (kubectl get deploy anomaly-api -n ml-serving). Lower than that means a pod exists but Prometheus cannot scrape it -- check kubectl get pods and the Kubernetes API server connectivity.

panels.title: API uptime (currently-serving process, minutes)
panels.description: Minutes since the OLDEST currently-running pod started. Resets to 0 on every rollout or pod restart -- this is informational, not a health signal by itself. A value that keeps resetting every few minutes without you deploying anything indicates pods are crash-looping.

panels.title: Feedback DB write p95
panels.description: 95th-percentile time spent writing ONE prediction to PostgreSQL (a slice of total /predict latency, see the p95-per-pod panel). Typically a few ms to tens of ms. If this climbs, /predict latency climbs with it even though the model itself is unchanged.

panels.title: Anomalous machines over time
panels.description: How many machines are anomalous right now (latest verdict per machine, from the pod that served it last, among machines that reported in the last 5 minutes and have not missed their reports), how many of them the classifier flagged (the machines the Telegram list names: a machine flagged by the IsolationForest safety net alone is not sent), and how many have missed their reports (silent for more than three of their usual intervals: the ⚫ lines of the Telegram list). The gap between the first two curves is the safety-net-only machines (Review tab). The second curve is the row count of the table below and of the Telegram list; it starts on 27 October 2026, when its rule was added. There is no fixed normal level: compare the curves with their own last hours. The FleetAnomalySurge alert reads the first curve: it fires when it is at least 20 and more than twice its 6-hour average for 2 minutes, which points at a router or a shared dependency (see Root cause below).

panels.title: Anomalous machines now (the Telegram list)
panels.description: The same machines as the Telegram anomaly list: every machine whose latest verdict is anomalous and was flagged by the classifier, from the pod that served it last, among machines that still report on time (a machine that missed its reports is in the table "Machines not reporting" instead; one flagged by the IsolationForest safety net alone is not listed, see the Review tab). A machine leaves the list on its first verdict that is not a confirmed anomaly. Its row count is the second curve above. The Telegram message is sent within 5 seconds of a change; this panel refreshes every 30 seconds.

panels.title: Classifier anomaly probability by machine (top 25)
panels.description: The 25 machines with the highest classifier P(anomaly) on their latest reading (from the pod that served them last, among machines that reported in the last 5 minutes), with the likely cause when the latest verdict is an anomaly; 'normal' = not flagged. The classifier flags a reading when P(normal) is below the decision threshold, i.e. P(anomaly) above 1 - threshold (0.09 at the served threshold 0.91; the threshold is in the model manifest, see /health, model_lineage). The IsolationForest safety net can flag a machine with a low P(anomaly) too.

targets.expr: sort_desc(topk(25, (max by (machine, cause) (api_anomaly_cause_p{job="anomaly-api-pods",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))) and on(machine) (time() - max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}) < 300)) or on(machine) label_replace((max by (machine) (api_classifier_p_anomaly{job="anomaly-api-pods",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))) and on(machine) (time() - max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}) < 300)), "cause", "normal", "", "")))

panels.title: Machines not reporting (the Telegram ⚫ lines)
panels.description: Machines that missed their reports: silent for more than three of their usual intervals (each machine's interval is measured from its own reports; at least 30 s, and 15 minutes while it is not known yet). The value is how long it has been silent. Its last verdict no longer counts as current, so it is not in the anomalous table. Empty when every machine reports on time; when every machine is here, the Telegram list says "no information".

panels.title: Fleet-wide average CPU
panels.description: Average of the raw CPU % each machine's most recent request (machines that reported in the last 5 minutes) actually reported (not a synthetic value -- literally what the API received). Purely descriptive of current fleet load; there is no fixed 'bad' threshold here since machine types have very different normal baselines (a database server idles hotter than a web server, by design of the synthetic generator).

targets.expr: avg((api_input_metric{job="anomaly-api-pods",feature="cpu",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))) and on(machine) (time() - max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}) < 300))

panels.title: Fleet-wide average network
panels.description: Average of the raw network MB/s each machine's most recent request (machines that reported in the last 5 minutes) reported. Same caveat as CPU: descriptive only, no universal threshold, since normal ranges differ by machine type.

targets.expr: avg((api_input_metric{job="anomaly-api-pods",feature="network",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))) and on(machine) (time() - max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}) < 300))

panels.title: Fleet-wide average load
panels.description: Average of the raw load-average value each machine's most recent request (machines that reported in the last 5 minutes) reported. Same caveat: descriptive, not a threshold -- a machine's OWN per-machine, per-time-window baseline (not this fleet-wide average) is what the model actually scores it against.

targets.expr: avg((api_input_metric{job="anomaly-api-pods",feature="load_avg",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))) and on(machine) (time() - max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}) < 300))

panels.title: Root cause spotlight (last 5 minutes)
panels.description: Routers the /root-cause analysis named as the LIKELY ORIGIN of a correlated failure (not just anomalous themselves) in the last 5 minutes, and how many times. The production agent sends the currently anomalous machines to /root-cause every 20 seconds, so about 15 checks happen in 5 minutes and the most this can show is 14 (Prometheus counts the steps between checks): 14 means the router was named in every check, i.e. for the whole 5 minutes; 1 means one check. Calls from the control panel's Root Cause tab count too. Only machines with dependents in dependency_graph.json (the routers) can appear. Empty is the normal state. The value is for now (the last 5 minutes), not for the dashboard's time range; the chart below shows when.

panels.title: Root cause events over time
panels.description: When each router was named the likely root cause: how many /root-cause checks named it in each minute. The production agent checks every 20 seconds, so the most is about 3 per minute: a line at 3 means the router was the root cause the whole minute, 0 means not at all. A router that keeps coming back stands out from a one-off. (A pod restart does not show as a drop: increase() handles counter resets.)

panels.title: Distinct anomalous machines (since pods started)
panels.description: How many DIFFERENT machines have been anomalous at least once since the current pods started (a Counter, so it only grows -- unlike the 'currently anomalous' panels above). Resets to 0 on every rollout. High relative to 200 over a long session is expected; a high value within minutes of startup would be unusual.

panels.title: Distinct root-cause machines (since pods started)
panels.description: Same idea as the panel to its left, but for root-cause incidents specifically: how many distinct machines have been identified as a likely root cause since the pods started.

panels.title: Host VM — CPU usage (real)
panels.description: Real CPU usage of the VM itself, not a machine in the simulated fleet. Sustained above ~90% is worth attention -- this VM also runs Jenkins, SonarQube, Minikube and every service at once, so high-but-brief spikes during a build or a training run are normal.

panels.title: Host VM — RAM available
panels.description: Real RAM still available on the VM. This project has hit genuine out-of-memory failures before (documented in the README's operational incidents) -- treat low single-digit GB as a real warning, not just a number. The MemoryLow alert (Telegram) fires below 1.5 GB available for 5 minutes.

panels.title: Host VM — Disk free (root)
panels.description: Real free disk space on the VM's root filesystem. This has genuinely caused a real incident before: Elasticsearch (inside SonarQube) went read-only and failed the Quality Gate when this dropped too low, fixed with docker image/builder prune. Below a few GB free is a real, previously-experienced risk on this exact VM, not a theoretical one. The DiskAlmostFull alert (Telegram) fires below 10% free for 5 minutes (this panel shows GB; the alert uses the percentage).

panels.title: Host VM — Load average (1m)
panels.description: Real 1-minute load average of the VM. As a rule of thumb, sustained load above the VM's CPU core count means more work is queued than the machine can run concurrently.

panels.title: Kubernetes — pod status
panels.description: Ready (1) / Not Ready (0) for every pod in ml-serving. Any pod stuck at 0 for more than a minute or two after a rollout usually means its readiness probe (GET /health) is failing -- check kubectl logs on that pod.

panels.title: Kubernetes — pod restart counts
panels.description: How many times each pod's container has restarted since it was created. 0 is normal. A number that keeps climbing means the container is crashing and Kubernetes is restarting it -- check kubectl describe pod for the reason (often an unhandled exception or a failed liveness probe).

panels.title: Kubernetes — replicas (desired vs available)
panels.description: Desired = what the Deployment (or the HPA, if it has scaled) asks for; Available = how many are actually ready right now. The two lines should track each other closely; a persistent gap means new pods are being scheduled but failing to become ready.

panels.title: Kubernetes — HPA CPU utilization
panels.description: Average CPU utilization the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is measuring across the anomaly-api pods. When this crosses the HPA's configured target (see kubernetes/deployment.yaml or the hpa.yaml manifest), Kubernetes adds replicas automatically; below it, replicas may scale back down.
